The river town woke before the shops did. At the end of the stone bridge a woman in a grey coat set a wooden crate of apples on the wall and watched the water move under the arches. She had walked this way every morning for years. A boy on a bicycle passed her, ringing his bell twice, and the sound bounced off the warehouses and came back thinner. Gulls stood on the pilings as if they had been posted there to count the boats.

By the time she reached the market square the light had climbed the roofs. The baker was already sliding trays onto the counter, and the smell of warm bread met the colder smell of the river. Two fishermen argued, without anger, about whether the tide would turn before noon. The woman bought a loaf and a paper of coffee. She did not hurry. The day ahead was ordinary, which was what she wanted from it: letters to answer, a leaking tap, a visit to her brother on the hill.

She sat for a while on the low wall beside the customs house and ate a piece of the bread. A barge moved upstream so slowly that the wake seemed to think before it spread. Nothing unusual was happening. The water was dark, steady, and full of small reflections of windows. When she stood up, crumbs fell onto the stones and the gulls came down at once. She folded the paper around the rest of the loaf and went on toward the hill, where the road narrowed and the town noise fell away behind her.
